claim: Spontaneous activity is a hallmark of developing neural systems.
source: Spontaneous activity is a hallmark of developing neural systems.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: In the retina, spontaneous activity comes in the form of retinal waves, comprised of three stages persisting from embryonic day 16 (E16) to eye opening at postnatal day 14 (P14).
source: In the retina, spontaneous activity comes in the form of retinal waves, comprised of three stages persisting from embryonic day 16 (E16) to eye opening at postnatal day 14 (P14).
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established literature on retinal waves.

claim: Stage 1 waves are initiated at several locations across the retina and propagate across a broad range of areas.
source: Using a custom-built macroscope to record spontaneous calcium transients from whole embryonic retinas, we show that stage 1 waves are initiated at several locations across the retina and propagate across a broad range of areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Blocking gap junctions reduced the frequency and size of stage 1 waves, nearly abolishing them.
source: Blocking gap junctions reduced the frequency and size of stage 1 waves, nearly abolishing them.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments with MFA shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Global blockade of nAChRs similarly nearly abolished stage 1 waves.
source: Global blockade of nAChRs similarly nearly abolished stage 1 waves.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments with hexamethonium and epibatidine shown in Figure 2I-L.

claim: Stage 1 waves are mediated by a complex circuitry involving subtypes of nAChRs and gap junctions.
source: Thus, stage 1 waves are mediated by a complex circuitry involving subtypes of nAChRs and gap junctions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological experiments presented in Figure 2.

claim: Stage 1 waves in mice lacking the β2 subunit of the nAChRs (β2-nAChR-KO) persisted with altered propagation properties.
source: Stage 1 waves in mice lacking the β2 subunit of the nAChRs (β2-nAChR-KO) persisted with altered propagation properties and were abolished by a gap junction blocker.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from β2-nAChR-KO mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Stage 1 waves in β2-nAChR-KO mice were abolished by a gap junction blocker.
source: Stage 1 waves in mice lacking the β2 subunit of the nAChRs (β2-nAChR-KO) persisted with altered propagation properties and were abolished by a gap junction blocker.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments in β2-nAChR-KO mice shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The developmental decrease in ipRGC density is preserved between WT and β2-nAChR-KO mice.
source: We found that the developmental decrease in ipRGC density is preserved between WT and β2-nAChR-KO mice, indicating that processes regulating ipRGC numbers and distributions are not influenced by spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is supported by ipRGC density measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Processes regulating ipRGC numbers and distributions are not influenced by spontaneous activity.
source: We found that the developmental decrease in ipRGC density is preserved between WT and β2-nAChR-KO mice, indicating that processes regulating ipRGC numbers and distributions are not influenced by spontaneous activity.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the ipRGC density data in WT and β2-nAChR-KO mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Retinal waves drive eye-specific segregation and retinotopic refinement of retinal projections to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus.
source: Retinal waves drive eye-specific segregation and retinotopic refinement of retinal projections to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus (Ackman and Crair, 2014; Arroyo and Feller, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retinal waves play a role in the maturation of direction-selectivity within the retina and superior colliculus.
source: Retinal waves also play a role in the maturation of direction-selectivity within the retina (Tiriac et al., 2022) and superior colliculus (Ge et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2009), as well as the development of retinal vasculature (Biswas et al., 2020; Weiner et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retinal waves play a role in the development of retinal vasculature.
source: Retinal waves also play a role in the maturation of direction-selectivity within the retina (Tiriac et al., 2022) and superior colliculus (Ge et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2009), as well as the development of retinal vasculature (Biswas et al., 2020; Weiner et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retinal waves are present throughout mouse retinal development, starting as early as embryonic day 16 and persisting until postnatal day 14.
source: Retinal waves are present throughout mouse retinal development, starting as early as embryonic day 16 and persisting until postnatal day 14, which is around the time of eye opening (Blankenship and Feller, 2010; Choi et al., 2021; Feller and Kerschensteiner, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stage 2 retinal waves, observed between postnatal day 1 and 10 (P1–10), are mediated via activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) by acetylcholine (ACh) released from starburst amacrine cells (SACs).
source: Stage 2 retinal waves, observed between postnatal day 1 and 10 (P1–10), are mediated via activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) by acetylcholine (ACh) released from starburst amacrine cells (SACs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stage 2 waves.

claim: Stage 3 retinal waves, observed between P10 and 14, are mediated via activation of ionotropic glutamate receptors by glutamate released from bipolar cells.
source: Stage 3 retinal waves, observed between P10 and 14, are mediated via activation of ionotropic glutamate receptors by glutamate released from bipolar cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stage 3 waves.

claim: Stage 1 waves are present in mice between embryonic day 16 and 18 (E16–18).
source: Stage 1 waves are present in mice between embryonic day 16 and 18 (E16–18) (Bansal et al., 2000) and in rabbit starting at E22 (Syed et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stage 1 waves are present in rabbit starting at E22.
source: Stage 1 waves are present in mice between embryonic day 16 and 18 (E16–18) (Bansal et al., 2000) and in rabbit starting at E22 (Syed et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In rabbit, stage 1 waves persist in the presence of pharmacological antagonists of fast neurotransmitters and are blocked by gap junction antagonists.
source: In rabbit, stage 1 waves persist in the presence of pharmacological antagonists of fast neurotransmitters and are blocked by gap junction antagonists (Syed et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In mice, stage 1 waves consist of large propagating waves and small non-propagating events.
source: In mice, stage 1 waves consist of large propagating waves and small non-propagating events (Bansal et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The application of nAChR antagonist inhibits larger propagating waves in mice.
source: The application of nAChR antagonist inhibits larger propagating waves (Bansal et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is no anatomical evidence of synapses as early as E16–18.
source: Though there is no anatomical evidence of synapses as early as E16–18, recent work has shown that SACs are present embryonically, begin to migrate to the inner nuclear layer (INL), and send projections to the inner plexiform layer (IPL) guided by homotypic contacts (Ray et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SACs are present embryonically, begin to migrate to the inner nuclear layer (INL), and send projections to the inner plexiform layer (IPL) guided by homotypic contacts.
source: Though there is no anatomical evidence of synapses as early as E16–18, recent work has shown that SACs are present embryonically, begin to migrate to the inner nuclear layer (INL), and send projections to the inner plexiform layer (IPL) guided by homotypic contacts (Ray et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cholinergic signaling is likely occurring via the volumetric release of ACh.
source: Hence, cholinergic signaling is likely occurring via the volumetric release of ACh (Ford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of synapses and the presence of SACs, supported by a citation.

claim: At E16–18, several postmitotic cell types are present in the retina, including broad classes of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and amacrine cells (ACs), as well as proliferating progenitors.
source: At E16–18, several postmitotic cell types are present in the retina, including broad classes of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and amacrine cells (ACs), as well as proliferating progenitors which will go on to produce cells such as rods, bipolar cells, and Muller glia postnatally (Figure 1A; Cepko, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: By E17, there are no chemical synaptic structures.
source: By E17, there are no chemical synaptic structures (Hoon et al., 2014), though migrating SACs release ACh (Wong, 1995), and they, along with RGCs, express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Migrating SACs release ACh at E17.
source: By E17, there are no chemical synaptic structures (Hoon et al., 2014), though migrating SACs release ACh (Wong, 1995), and they, along with RGCs, express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SACs and RGCs express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at E17.
source: By E17, there are no chemical synaptic structures (Hoon et al., 2014), though migrating SACs release ACh (Wong, 1995), and they, along with RGCs, express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Gap junction coupling between RGCs and between progenitor cells is a potential mode of cell–cell communication during stage 1 waves.
source: One potential mode of cell–cell communication is via gap junction coupling between RGCs as well as between progenitor cells (Cook and Becker, 2009), which have been proposed to be the primary substrate mediating stage 1 waves (Catsicas et al., 1998; Syed et al., 2004; Wong et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gap junction coupling has been proposed to be the primary substrate mediating stage 1 waves.
source: One potential mode of cell–cell communication is via gap junction coupling between RGCs as well as between progenitor cells (Cook and Becker, 2009), which have been proposed to be the primary substrate mediating stage 1 waves (Catsicas et al., 1998; Syed et al., 2004; Wong et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The earliest age at which reliable waves could be detected was E16.
source: The earliest age at which we could detect reliable waves was E16 (Video 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Video 1.

claim: The distribution of inter-transient intervals (ITI) for stage 1 waves peaked at around 80 s.
source: We first computed the time between spontaneous transients by measuring the inter-transient interval (ITI) for each ROI and found that the distribution peaked at around 80 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The distribution of wave sizes ranged from 6 to 90% of the retina, with a mean and standard deviation of 46 ± 21%.
source: The distribution of wave sizes was broad, ranging from 6 to 90% of the retina, with a mean and standard deviation of 46 ± 21% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Small non-propagating calcium events were observed in addition to propagating waves.
source: In addition to propagating waves, we also observed small non-propagating calcium events (defined by transients present in a few neighboring ROIs that never propagated beyond 160 × 160 μm2; Video 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Video 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average propagation speed of stage 1 waves ranged from 145 μm/s to 237 μm/s (average ± SD: 181 ± 24 μm/s).
source: Finally, we calculated the average propagation speed of stage 1 waves to range from 145 μm/s to 237 μm/s (average ± SD: 181 ± 24 μm/s; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar to stage 2 waves we observed with an average speed of 177 μm/s ± 62 μm/s (see Table 1 for wave speed summary data).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: Stage 1 wave propagation speed is similar to stage 2 wave propagation speed (177 μm/s ± 62 μm/s).
source: Finally, we calculated the average propagation speed of stage 1 waves to range from 145 μm/s to 237 μm/s (average ± SD: 181 ± 24 μm/s; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar to stage 2 waves we observed with an average speed of 177 μm/s ± 62 μm/s (see Table 1 for wave speed summary data).
evidence: This is based on data comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: There was no evidence of an initiation site bias for stage 1 waves in WT retinas.
source: We also measured the distribution of stage 1 wave initiation sites in WT retinas and saw no evidence of an initiation site bias (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Application of the gap junction blocker MFA (50 μM) nearly abolished stage 1 waves, causing a significant reduction in frequency of waves and cell participation during waves.
source: Application of the gap junction blocker MFA (50 μM) nearly abolished stage 1 waves, causing a significant reduction in frequency of waves and cell participation during waves (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: MFA caused a small but significant reduction in wave amplitude.
source: We also found a small but significant reduction in wave amplitude, quantified as the average maximum response amplitude of all cells participating in individual waves (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DHβE dramatically reduced activity associated with stage 1 retinal waves.
source: We found that DHβE also dramatically reduced activity associated with stage 1 retinal waves (Figure 2E-H).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: In the presence of DHβE, some waves persisted but recruited fewer neurons and had smaller areas.
source: However, in contrast to stage 2, some waves persisted in the presence of DHβE, but recruited fewer neurons and therefore had smaller areas (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Hexamethonium (Hex, 100 μM) blocked stage 1 wave events.
source: Stage 1 waves were blocked by general nAChR antagonists: both hexamethonium (Figure 2I-J; Hex, 100 μM), a non-selective nAChR antagonist, and epibatidine (Figure 2K-L; EPB, 10 nM), an nAChR agonist that potently desensitizes all nAChRs (Corrie et al., 2020; Spang et al., 2000), blocked stage 1 wave events.
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Epibatidine (EPB, 10 nM) blocked stage 1 wave events.
source: Stage 1 waves were blocked by general nAChR antagonists: both hexamethonium (Figure 2I-J; Hex, 100 μM), a non-selective nAChR antagonist, and epibatidine (Figure 2K-L; EPB, 10 nM), an nAChR agonist that potently desensitizes all nAChRs (Corrie et al., 2020; Spang et al., 2000), blocked stage 1 wave events.
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2K-L.

claim: Both gap junctions and multiple subunit combinations of nAChRs mediate the initiation and propagation of stage 1 waves.
source: Hence, both gap junctions and multiple subunit combinations of nAChRs mediate the initiation and propagation of stage 1 waves .
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological experiments presented in Figure 2.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO mice have severely disrupted stage 2 retinal waves.
source: β2-nAChR-KO mice have severely disrupted stage 2 retinal waves (Bansal et al., 2000; Rossi et al., 2001) and have served as a model system for assessing the role of stage 2 waves in driving different developmental events (Ackman et al., 2012; Burbridge et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO mice have served as a model system for assessing the role of stage 2 waves in driving different developmental events.
source: β2-nAChR-KO mice have severely disrupted stage 2 retinal waves (Bansal et al., 2000; Rossi et al., 2001) and have served as a model system for assessing the role of stage 2 waves in driving different developmental events (Ackman et al., 2012; Burbridge et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited stage 1 waves with different spatiotemporal properties than those of WT retinas.
source: We observed that β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited stage 1 waves with different spatiotemporal properties than those of WT retinas (Figure 3A and B, see also Video 3).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B and Video 3.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited longer inter-event intervals (IEIs) than WT retinas.
source: Specifically, β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited longer IEIs (Figure 3C and D), and individual waves propagated over smaller areas β2-nAChR-KO (Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Individual waves in β2-nAChR-KO retinas propagated over smaller areas than in WT retinas.
source: Specifically, β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited longer IEIs (Figure 3C and D), and individual waves propagated over smaller areas β2-nAChR-KO (Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Waves in the β2-nAChR-KO retina were unaffected by the addition of Hex.
source: In sharp contrast to WT retina, waves in the β2-nAChR-KO retina were unaffected by the addition of Hex but showed a significant reduction in both area and frequency with the application of MFA (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Waves in the β2-nAChR-KO retina showed a significant reduction in both area and frequency with the application of MFA.
source: In sharp contrast to WT retina, waves in the β2-nAChR-KO retina were unaffected by the addition of Hex but showed a significant reduction in both area and frequency with the application of MFA (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: In the absence of β2-nAChRs, gap junctions are the primary remaining component of the stage 1 wave generation mechanism.
source: These results suggest that in the absence of β2-nAChRs, gap junctions are the primary remaining component of the stage 1 wave generation mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pharmacological experiments in β2-nAChR-KO mice.

claim: Stage 1 waves in the β2-nAChR-KO propagated at a significantly slower speed than those observed in WT mice (average ± SD: 99 ± 15 µm/s compared to 181 ± 24 µm/s for WT).
source: Furthermore, we found that stage 1 waves in the β2-nAChR-KO propagated at a significantly slower speed than those observed in WT mice (average ± SD: 99 ± 15 µm/s compared to 181 ± 24 µm/s for WT, n = 10 waves per condition, p=3.9073e–8) (Figure 3F), consistent with a distinct mechanism of propagation.
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The slower propagation speed of stage 1 waves in β2-nAChR-KO mice is consistent with a distinct mechanism of propagation.
source: Furthermore, we found that stage 1 waves in the β2-nAChR-KO propagated at a significantly slower speed than those observed in WT mice (average ± SD: 99 ± 15 µm/s compared to 181 ± 24 µm/s for WT, n = 10 waves per condition, p=3.9073e–8) (Figure 3F), consistent with a distinct mechanism of propagation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the wave speed data.

claim: There was no difference in the frequency of waves recorded using a two-photon microscope to those recorded on the macroscope in either the WT or β2 nAChR-KO embryonic retinas.
source: However, we found no difference in the frequency of waves recorded using a two-photon microscope (based on 920 nm illumination) to those recorded on the macroscope and in either the WT or β2 nAChR-KO embryonic retinas (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on data comparison shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light activation of ipRGCs does not significantly influence the spatiotemporal properties of stage 1 retinal waves in either WT or the β2 nAChR-KO retinas.
source: Hence, we conclude that light activation of ipRGCs does not significantly influence the spatiotemporal properties of stage 1 retinal waves in either WT or the β2 nAChR-KO retinas.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of wave frequencies under different imaging conditions.

claim: Light stimulation of the retina does not modulate the frequency of stage 2 waves and only begins to do so when conventional photoreceptors come online during stage 3 waves.
source: These results are consistent with the fact that light stimulation of the retina does not modulate the frequency of stage 2 waves and only begins to do so when conventional photoreceptors come online during stage 3 waves (Tiriac et al., 2018, Renna et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RGCs undergo a period of dramatic cell death during the first two postnatal weeks of development, the majority occurring during the first postnatal week.
source: RGCs undergo a period of dramatic cell death during the first two postnatal weeks of development, the majority occurring during the first postnatal week (Abed et al., 2022; Braunger et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ipRGCs have completed proliferation and appear to be fully differentiated by E16.
source: First, ipRGCs have completed proliferation (Lucas and Schmidt, 2019; McNeill et al., 2011) and appear to be fully differentiated by E16 (Shekhar et al., 2022; Whitney et al., 2022), the onset of stage 1 waves.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ipRGCs undergo a period of dramatic cell death during the first two postnatal weeks of development, the majority occurring during the first postnatal week.
source: ipRGCs undergo a period of dramatic cell death during the first two postnatal weeks of development, the majority occurring during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Prevention of cell death profoundly disrupts several important developmental processes in the retina – including spacing of ipRGC somas as well as rod- and cone-mediated circadian entrainment through the activation of ipRGCs.
source: Prevention of cell death profoundly disrupts several important developmental processes in the retina – including spacing of ipRGC somas as well as rod- and cone-mediated circadian entrainment through the activation of ipRGCs (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both RGCs and ipRGCs participated in most waves with no significant differences between the two groups (average ± SD: RGCs 78.78 ± 21.48%; ipRGCs 84.64 ± 16.86%).
source: On average, both RGCs and ipRGCs participated in most waves with no significant differences between the two groups (Figure 4C; average ± SD: RGCs 78.78 ± 21.48%; ipRGCs 84.64 ± 16.86%).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were no significant differences in the amplitude of the calcium response that RGCs and ipRGCs exhibit in response to stage 1 waves.
source: We also found no significant differences in the amplitude of the calcium response that RGCs and ipRGCs exhibit in response to stage 1 waves (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ipRGCs are depolarized by stage 1 waves similarly to stage 2 waves.
source: Hence, ipRGCs are depolarized by stage 1 waves similarly to stage 2 waves (Caval-Holme et al., 2019; Caval-Holme et al., 2022; Chew et al., 2017).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the participation data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A dramatic decrease in the density of ipRGCs was observed in WT retinas from P1 to P7.
source: We observed a dramatic decrease in the density of ipRGCs in WT retinas from P1 to P7 (Figure 5B and C; p=1.17 × 10–7), consistent with previous studies of ipRGCs (Chen et al., 2013) and which coincides with peak levels of RGC apoptosis, the primary cause of RGC death during development (Braunger et al., 2014; Young, 1984).
evidence: This is based on ipRGC density measurements shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The decrease in ipRGC density from P1 to P7 is consistent with previous studies of ipRGCs and coincides with peak levels of RGC apoptosis.
source: We observed a dramatic decrease in the density of ipRGCs in WT retinas from P1 to P7 (Figure 5B and C; p=1.17 × 10–7), consistent with previous studies of ipRGCs (Chen et al., 2013) and which coincides with peak levels of RGC apoptosis, the primary cause of RGC death during development (Braunger et al., 2014; Young, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited the same density of ipRGCs at P1 as WT retinas.
source: We found that β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited the same density of ipRGCs at P1 as WT retinas, suggesting that the decrease in activity in stage 1 waves does not regulate ipRGC cell density.
evidence: This is based on ipRGC density measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The decrease in activity in stage 1 waves does not regulate ipRGC cell density.
source: We found that β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited the same density of ipRGCs at P1 as WT retinas, suggesting that the decrease in activity in stage 1 waves does not regulate ipRGC cell density.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ipRGC density data.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO retinas exhibited a decrease in the density of ipRGCs from P1 to P7.
source: Like WTs, β2-nAChR-KO retinas also exhibited a decrease in the density of ipRGCs from P1 to P7 (p=4.99 × 10–11).
evidence: This is based on ipRGC density measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At P7, there was a small but significant increase in ipRGC densities in β2-nAChR-KO mice than in WT mice (568 ± 33 ipRGCs/µm2 in WT vs. 654 ± 78 ipRGCs/µm2 in β2-nAChR-KO).
source: At P7, we observed a small but significant increase in ipRGC densities at P7 in β2-nAChR-KO mice than in WT mice (568 ± 33 ipRGCs/µm2 in WT vs. 654 ± 78 ipRGCs/µm2 in β2-nAChR-KO, n = 8 retinas in each genotype).
evidence: This is based on ipRGC density measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The cell death processes that regulate ipRGC density during the first postnatal week persist despite a significant reduction in wave activity.
source: Overall, these data indicate that the cell death processes that regulate ipRGC density during the first postnatal week persist despite a significant reduction in wave activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ipRGC density data in WT and β2-nAChR-KO mice.

claim: Despite the expected increase in nearest-neighbor distance in WT and β2-nAChR-KOs retina between P1 and P7, there was only a small decrease in the regularity index.
source: Despite the expected increase in nearest-neighbor distance in WT and β2-nAChR-KOs retina between P1 and P7 (Figure 5D, see Table 2), there was only a small decrease in the regularity index.
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 5D and Table 2.

claim: The measured mean regularity indices fall within the range of what would be predicted by a random distribution of cells with soma diameters between 7–10 μm.
source: Interestingly, the measured mean regularity indices of 2.8 ± 0.12 (WT P1), 2.9 ± 0.16 (β2-nAChR-KO P1), 2.3 ± 0.13 (WT P7) and 2.6 ± 0.2 (β2-nAChR-KO P1) fall within the range of what would be predicted by a random distribution of cells with soma diameters between 7–10 μm (Keeley et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The decrease in cell density does not appear to make the soma organization more ordered.
source: Hence, the decrease in cell density does not appear make the soma organization more ordered.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the regularity index data.

claim: Although retinal waves provide a robust source of depolarization for embryonic and early postnatal ipRGCs, reducing wave activity does not significantly influence the processes that regulate their density or organization.
source: Together these data indicate that although retinal waves provide a robust source of depolarization for embryonic and early postnatal ipRGCs, reducing wave activity does not significantly influence the processes that regulate their density or organization.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the ipRGC density and regularity data.

claim: Stage 1 waves are a robust source of spontaneous activity in the embryonic retina.
source: We show that stage 1 retinal waves are a robust source of spontaneous activity in the embryonic retina.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Stage 1 waves initiate throughout the retina, propagate over finite regions of varying size, and drive periodic depolarizations of neurons in the immature retinal GCL.
source: Stage 1 waves initiate throughout the retina, propagate over finite regions of varying size, and drive periodic depolarizations of neurons in the immature retinal GCL.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: In WT embryonic mice, stage 1 waves are abolished in the presence of general nAChR antagonists.
source: In WT embryonic mice, stage 1 waves are abolished in the presence of general nAChR antagonists but persist, albeit with greatly reduced cell participation, in an nAChR antagonist that targets α4β2 containing nAChRs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Stage 1 waves persist, albeit with greatly reduced cell participation, in an nAChR antagonist that targets α4β2 containing nAChRs.
source: In WT embryonic mice, stage 1 waves are abolished in the presence of general nAChR antagonists but persist, albeit with greatly reduced cell participation, in an nAChR antagonist that targets α4β2 containing nAChRs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: In the presence of gap junction antagonists, the frequency and participation of cells within waves is greatly diminished, though some waves still occur.
source: In the presence of gap junction antagonists, the frequency and participation of cells within waves is also greatly diminished, though some waves still occur.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: In retinas isolated from embryonic β2-nAChR-KO mice, waves persisted both in control conditions and in the presence of a general nAChR antagonist, though the area of waves is greatly diminished compared to WT.
source: We found that in retinas isolated from embryonic β2-nAChR-KO mice, which exhibit strongly reduced stage 2 wave frequency, waves persisted both in control conditions and in the presence of a general nAChR antagonist, though the area of waves is greatly diminished compared to WT.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: The frequency of stage 1 waves in β2-nAChR-KO mice was greatly reduced in the presence of a gap junction antagonist.
source: However, similar to what we observed in WT mice, the frequency of stage 1 waves in β2-nAChR-KO mice was greatly reduced in the presence of a gap junction antagonist.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: The more striking effect of the gap junction antagonist compared to the general nAChR antagonist indicates that the electrical synapses are sufficient to generate waves in β2-nAChR-KO mice.
